# Gnathostomiasis

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Infectious diseases > Parasitic infections > Gnathostomiasis*

[Original Article Link](/library/M90MLR)

---

## Summary

Gnathostomiasis is a food-borne <u>zoonotic disease</u> caused by the <u>third-stage larvae</u> of Gnathostoma <u>nematodes</u>. It is <u>endemic</u> to regions such as Asia and Central and South America and is transmitted primarily through ingestion of raw or undercooked intermediate hosts (e.g., frogs, birds, freshwater fish). The clinical presentation is classified as either cutaneous or <u>visceral</u>. Cutaneous gnathostomiasis, the most common form, is characterized by intermittent, migratory subcutaneous swelling. <u>Visceral</u> gnathostomiasis involves larval migration to internal organs, which can lead to severe complications (e.g., <u>vision loss</u>). <u>Central nervous system</u> (<u>CNS</u>) involvement is known as neurognathostomiasis and is a life-threatening form of the disease. Diagnosis is based on clinical features, peripheral <u>eosinophilia</u>, and a relevant exposure history, with confirmation via <u>biopsy</u> or <u>serology</u>. Management includes surgical removal of larvae and/or pharmacological treatment (e.g., <u>albendazole</u>). Relapse is common and may require further treatment courses. Prevention focuses on avoiding consumption of raw or undercooked intermediate hosts.
